Save a panel exactly like the published datasets, ready to share or contribute.

## Parameters {.doc-section .doc-section-parameters}

| Name        | Type         | Description                                                              | Default       |
|-------------|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------|
| df          | pd.DataFrame | A valid panel (see ``geo.check``)                                        | _required_    |
| name        | str          | The dataset id: lowercase letters, digits, ``-`` or ``_``                | _required_    |
| scale       | str          | Its scale                                                                | _required_    |
| directory   |              | Where to write ``data/`` and ``metadata/`` (default: the current folder) | `'.'`         |
| title       | str \| None  | What the dataset is                                                      | `None`        |
| description | str \| None  | What the dataset is                                                      | `None`        |
| variables   | dict \| None | ``{column: {"label", "description", "unit", "aggregation", "source"}}``  | `None`        |
| sources     |              | Titles or ``{"title", "path"}`` dicts of the sources                     | `()`          |
| citation    | str \| None  | The recommended citation                                                 | `None`        |
| license     | str          | An SPDX license id (default ``CC-BY-4.0``)                               | `'CC-BY-4.0'` |

## Notes {.doc-section .doc-section-notes}

Writes ``<directory>/data/<scale>/<name>.csv`` and ``.parquet`` and
``<directory>/metadata/<name>.datapackage.json`` (Frictionless). Describe each
variable in ``variables``: ``{"pop": {"label": "Population", "description":
"Sum of WorldPop 100 m population over the unit", "unit": "people",
"aggregation": "sum", "source": "WorldPop"}}``. The ``label`` is a readable
name for plots; the description says how the variable was built. The
aggregation rule (``sum``, ``mean``, ``weighted_mean:<field>``, ``none``, ...)
tells ``geo.aggregate()`` how to move the variable to coarser scales.

Returns the datapackage as a dict.

## Example {.doc-section .doc-section-example}

```python
!pip install -q "geo4bolivia[raster]"
import numpy as np
import rasterio
from rasterio.transform import from_bounds
import geo4bolivia as geo
import plotly.express as px

# A small raster of rough distance to La Paz (km); use your own GeoTIFF instead
x0, y0, x1, y1 = geo.boundaries("country").total_bounds
lon, lat = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x0, x1, 400), np.linspace(y1, y0, 400))
km = 111 * np.hypot(lon + 68.13, lat + 16.50)
with rasterio.open("dist.tif", "w", driver="GTiff", width=400, height=400,
                   count=1, dtype="float32", crs="EPSG:4326",
                   transform=from_bounds(x0, y0, x1, y1, 400, 400)) as f:
    f.write(km.astype("float32"), 1)

dist = geo.zonal("dist.tif", scale="province", stats=["mean"],
                 name="dist_lpz", year=2024)
pkg = geo.save(dist, "distance", scale="province", directory="my_data",
               title="Distance to La Paz",
               variables={"dist_lpz_mean": {"label": "Distance to La Paz (km)",
                          "unit": "km", "aggregation": "none"}})
print(pkg["resources"][0]["schema"]["fields"][2])
```
